## About

In this slides we discuss why global package installation breaks reproducibility.

- [The Dependency Problem:]{.bold-hilit} Different projects require different versions of the same library.

- [Global Pollution:]{.bold-hilit} Installing packages globally eventually creates conflicting version requirements.

- [The Solution:]{.bold-hilit} Isolated directories containing specific language runtimes and library versions.


# Intro

## Common Problems

- A research project requires different versions of your base programming languages 
(or different versions from the ones you are currently using).

- An application you developed as part of a previous research project that 
worked fine on your system six months ago now no longer works.

- Code that was written for a joint research project works on your machine 
but not on your collaborators' machines.

- An application that you are developing on your local machine doesn't provide 
the same results when run on your remote cluster.


## Some Difficulties

Installing software system-wide has a number of drawbacks:

- It can be difficult to figure out what software is required for any particular research project.

- It is often impossible to install different versions of the same software package at the same time.

- Updating software required for one project can often “break” the software installed for another project.


## Some Vocabulary

- [Module:]{.bold-hilit} A collection of functions and variables, as in a script.
    + Note: The term _Module_ is not commonly used in the R community.

- [Package:]{.bold-hilit} A collection of modules, as in a directory with scripts.

- [Library:]{.bold-hilit} A collection of packages, typically stored in one directory.

- [_Warning:_]{.mdlit} Package and Library are often used interchangeably---even 
though they are different things.


## Some Vocabulary

Environment

- The word "environment" is heavily overloaded in computer science, and programming parlance.

- For the scope of this lecture, by environment we usually mean a "private sandbox to 
manage packages in a given project"

- An environment is NOT: 
    + a separate piece of software running on your computer,
    + a virtual machine

- Note; There is not a unique/universal definition of the term environment.


## Environment Management Systems

- Environment management systems help resolve dependency issues by allowing you to 
use different versions of a package for different projects.

- Make your projects self-contained and reproducible by capturing all package 
dependencies in a single requirements file.



# How R Handles Packages by Default

## Where Do Packages Live?

- In R, a "Library" is simply a directory (folder) on the computer where package files are stored. 
- R searches these directories to find the packages you ask for.
- By default, R uses a [system library]{.hilit} and a [user library]{.mdlit}. 
- You can see where these are on your machine by running this command in the R console:

. . .

```r
.libPaths()
```


## The Default Behavior 

- [System Library:]{.bold-hilit} Contains core packages that come pre-installed with R (e.g., `base`, `stats`, `utils`).

- [User Library:]{.bold-hilit} A single, global folder where all packages installed via `install.packages()` are placed.

- [The Shared Problem:]{.bold-hilit} Every R project on that computer shares this exact same User Library.


## What Happens when you run:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
`install.packages("ggplot2")`

- R connects to a remote cloud repository (like CRAN).
- It downloads a compressed file containing the `"ggplot2"` code.
- It unzips and builds those files.
- It drops the resulting `"ggplot2"` folder into the global User Library folder found in `.libPaths()`.
:::

::: {.column .fragment}
`library(ggplot2)`

- R stops looking at the cloud.
- It looks inside the folders listed in `.libPaths()`.
- It searches for a folder named _ggplot2_.
- It loads that package's functions into the computer's active RAM memory so they can use them.
:::
::::


## The Core Issue: Why This Breaks Reproducibility

Because there is only one global User Library, your computer can only hold one version 
of a package at a time. 

. . .

This creates two classic failure modes:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
Scenario A: 

- You write a script in 2024 using dplyr version 1.0.
- In 2026, you run `install.packages("dplyr")` for a new project, which updates it to version 1.2.
- Your 2024 script now crashes because functions changed or were deprecated in the new version.
:::

::: {.column .fragment}
Scenario B:

- You share a script with a colleague.
- The script crashes on their machine because their global User Library has an older or newer version of a package than yours does.
- The script itself contains no record of which version it actually needs to run.
:::
::::


## Shifting to Project-Local Libraries with `"renv"`

- `"renv"` fundamentally changes `.libPaths()`.
- Instead of pointing to a shared global folder, `"renv"` forces R to look at a private, isolated library folder inside that specific project directory.

. . .

```
[Standard R Workflow]
Project A ---\
              +---> Global User Library (One version of a package for everyone)
Project B ---/

[renv Workflow]
Project A --------> Private Library A (Isolated package versions)
Project B --------> Private Library B (Isolated package versions)
```


# Package `"renv"`

## Enter renv

`renv` stands for **Reproducible Environments**. 

Instead of using one global folder for everything, `renv` creates a 
**private library** inside your specific project.


## The Three Pillars of renv

`renv` relies on three core components to make your project reproducible:

1. [The Project Library:]{.bold-hilit} A private directory containing your project's packages.

2. [The Lockfile (`renv.lock`):]{.bold-hilit} A text file recording exact version numbers.

3. [The Infrastructure:]{.bold-hilit} Invisible scripts that configure R when the project opens.


## How renv Modifies your Project

When you run `renv::init()`, it adds a few files to your project folder:

* `renv/library/`: The folder where your project's packages are installed.
* `renv.lock`: The master ledger of your package versions.
* `.Rprofile`: A hidden script that R runs automatically every time the project opens.


## The Magic of `.Rprofile`

How does R know to stop looking at the global library?

1. You open your `.Rproj` file.
2. R looks for a file named `.Rprofile` and runs it immediately.
3. `renv` uses this file to temporarily rewrite your `.libPaths()`.
4. For the rest of your session, `install.packages()` and `library()` only look inside your private `renv/library/` folder.


# The Core Workflow

## Three Commands

You only need to learn three core commands for daily use:

1. `renv::init()` — Turn on environment tracking for a new project.
2. `renv::snapshot()` — Save the current package versions to the lockfile.
3. `renv::restore()` — Recreate the exact environment on a different computer.


## Step 1: `renv::init()`

What happens under the hood?

- `renv` scans your project scripts for `library()` or `require()` statements.
- It unlinks your project from the global user library.
- It creates your local `renv/library/`.
- It automatically takes your first "snapshot" to build the lockfile.


## Step 2: `renv::snapshot()`

Think of this as **saving your game progress**. 

- You install a new package using `install.packages()`.
- The files go into your private `renv/library/`.
- Running `renv::snapshot()` updates the `renv.lock` file with the exact version, 
package name, and download source (e.g., CRAN or GitHub).


## Inside a `renv.lock` File

The [lockfile]{.hilit} is just a human-readable text file (JSON format). 

. . .

It looks like this:

```json
{
  "R": { "Version": "4.3.2" },
  "Packages": {
    "ggplot2": {
      "Package": "ggplot2",
      "Version": "3.4.4",
      "Source": "Repository",
      "Repository": "CRAN"
    }
  }
}
```

*Perfect for tracking with Git!*


## Step 3: `renv::restore()`

How a collaborator (or future you) reproduces your work:

1. They download your project folder (which contains `renv.lock` and `.Rprofile`).
2. They open the project. R sees `.Rprofile` and activates `renv`.
3. They run `renv::restore()`.
4. R reads the `renv.lock` file and automatically downloads and installs the exact versions listed.


# Demo


# Behind the Scenes

## The Global Cache

**Concern:** *"If every project has its own library, won't I waste gigabytes of hard drive space reinstalling ggplot2 for every project?"*

. . .

**The Answer:** No! `renv` uses a hidden **Global Cache**.

- `renv` installs packages into a single central cache folder on your computer.
- It then creates a **symbolic link** (a shortcut) from your project's `renv/library/` to that cache.
- **Result:** Total isolation, but zero wasted disk space.


# Key Considerations: renv + Git

## What to Commit vs. What to Ignore

`"renv"` actually makes this easy by automatically generating a custom `.gitignore` file inside the 
`renv/` directory when you run `renv::init()`. 


## Always Commit (Track these text files in Git)

These files constitute the "recipe" for your environment. 

- `renv.lock`: The master ledger containing explicit package versions and sources.
- `.Rprofile`: The configuration script that forces R to activate `"renv"` when the project boots up.
- `renv/activate.R`: The internal engine script that `.Rprofile` calls to initialize the local environment paths.
- `renv/settings.json`: Project-specific settings for `"renv"` behavior.


## Never Commit (Ignore these in Git)

These folders contain the actual compiled software binary files ("the ingredients").

- `renv/library/`: This folder contains thousands of heavy, binary machine files.
- Why ignore it? It will bloat your Git repo to gigabytes. 
- Furthermore, binaries compiled on a Mac will completely fail if cloned onto a Windows machine.
- `renv/staging/`: Temporary directories used during package installation.
- `renv/cache/`: Project-specific caching artifacts.


## The Danger of Overwriting `.Rprofile`

- Many Git users or platform templates provide a global `.Rprofile` to auto-load specific settings.

- `"renv"` relies entirely on a project-local `.Rprofile` to hijack `.libPaths()`.

- If you blindly overwrite the `.Rprofile` generated by `"renv"` with your own custom setup, 
`"renv"` will fail to activate.

- Append your personal configurations to the bottom of the renv-generated `.Rprofile` instead of replacing it.


## Visualizing the Problem: Global Pollution

Without `renv`, your projects share one fragile ecosystem. A single package upgrade can cause a chain reaction.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    subgraph Computer [Your Computer]
        G[Global User Library] -->|v1.0| D[dplyr]
        
        subgraph ProjA [Project A: Written in 2024]
            A[analysis.R] -->|Depends on v1.0| G
        end
        
        subgraph ProjB [Project B: New in 2026]
            B[model.R] -->|Upgrades library to v1.2| G
        end
    end
    
    style A fill:#d4edda,stroke:#28a745
    style B fill:#f8d7da,stroke:#dc3545
    style G fill:#fff3cd,stroke:#ffc107
```


## Sample Project

```
my_project/
├── 📄 my_script.R        <-- Your analytical code
├── 📄 my_project.Rproj   <-- RStudio Project file
├── 📄 .Rprofile          <-- The invisible switch (Tells R to use renv)
├── 📄 renv.lock          <-- The recipe ledger (JSON package list)
└── 📁 renv/
├── 📄 activate.R     <-- The engine script
└── 📁 library/       <-- The local package storage (Git Ignored)
```


## The 3 Steps: A Visual Lifecycle

This loop represents the entire lifecycle of a reproducible project, from birth to sharing on GitHub.

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    Init(1. renv::init) --> Work[Write Code &<br>Install Packages]
    Work --> Snap(2. renv::snapshot)
    Snap --> Git[Commit & Push<br>renv.lock to Git]
    Git --> Rest(3. renv::restore)
    Rest -->|On Collaborator Machine| Work
    
    style Init fill:#e2e3e5,stroke:#383d41
    style Snap fill:#fff3cd,stroke:#ffc107
    style Rest fill:#d4edda,stroke:#28a745
```

---

## Visualizing Step 1: `renv::init()`

What happens when you turn `renv` on? It clones your existing context, boots up the local infrastructure, and saves your baseline state.

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    actor User
    participant R as R Session
    participant FS as Project Files
    
    User->>R: renv::init()
    R->>FS: Scans scripts for library() statements
    R->>FS: Generates .Rprofile & renv/ folder
    R->>FS: Creates first renv.lock file
    R-->>User: "Project initialized successfully!"
```

---

## Visualizing Step 2: `renv::snapshot()`

Your local package folder holds the heavy software binary files. Your lockfile holds the text description. `snapshot()` keeps them aligned.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    subgraph Hard Drive [Your Hard Drive]
        Lib[📁 renv/library/<br>Heavy Binary Files<br>Cannot be sent to GitHub]
        Lock[📄 renv.lock<br>Lightweight Text File<br>Perfect for GitHub]
    end

    User[User installs packages] -->|Modifies| Lib
    User -->|Runs renv::snapshot| Sync[renv reads local library]
    Sync -->|Writes exact versions into| Lock
    Lock -->|Pushed by User| GitHub(☁️ GitHub Repository)
    
    style Lib fill:#f8d7da,stroke:#dc3545
    style Lock fill:#d4edda,stroke:#28a745
    style GitHub fill:#e1becf,stroke:#6f42c1
```

---

## Visualizing Step 3: `renv::restore()`

When a collaborator pulls your code down, they don't have your packages. They read your lockfile to rebuild them locally from scratch.

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    Collab[Collaborator Clones Repo] --> Lock[📄 renv.lock]
    Lock --> Run[Runs renv::restore]
    Run --> CRAN[☁️ Fetch from CRAN / GitHub]
    CRAN --> Build[Builds custom 📁 renv/library/]
    Build --> Ready[🚀 Script runs with 0 errors]
    
    style Lock fill:#d4edda,stroke:#28a745
    style Ready fill:#d4edda,stroke:#28a745
```
